questions.question: What was the Bretton Woods system, established as an effect of the war? / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Bretton Woods system (1944) established postwar global economic order- creating the IMF
  • and World Bank to ensure monetary stability, fixed exchange rates pegged to the U.S. dollar,
  • and promote international trade and reconstruction after World War II.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Explain the principle of "collective security." / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Principle of collective security means that an attack on one state is considered an attack on
  • all, requiring joint action to preserve peace —seen in institutions like the League of Nations
  • and the United Nations.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: What kind of methods did the behaviouralists of the Second Debate champion for the study of IR? Discuss briefly. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Debates between Traditionalists and the Behaviouralists-methodologies of traditionalism
  • versus scientism-the former believed a historical and interpretive approach was necessary to
  • understand the complexity of world politics - the later promoted scientific, empirical, and
  • quantitative methods —surveys, statistical analysis, and hypothesis testing —to make
  • International Relations more objective, predictive, and systematic, moving away from
  • normative or historical approaches.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: How did the aftermath of World War I influence the emergence of International Relations as an academic discipline? / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• World War I’s devastation spurred efforts to understand and prevent future wars, leading
  • to the academic study of International Relations emphasizing peace, diplomacy, and
  • institutions—exemplified by the founding of the first IR chair at Aberystwyth in 1919.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Differentiate briefly between the realist and liberal traditions in IR using Hobbes and Kant. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Realism, rooted in Hobbes, views human nature as self -interested and conflictual,
  • prioritizing power and survival -Liberalism, inspired by Kant, stresses cooperation, moral
  • progress, and institutions to achieve perpetual peace through collective action and mutual
  • interdependence.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Describe how neoliberalism shapes the meaning of globalisation. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Neoliberalism views globalization as a process driven by market liberalization, free trade,
  • and deregulation- enhancing efficiency and global interdependence -frames globalization as
  • inevitable and beneficial through integration of economies and minimal state intervention.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: What is the G20, and why is it significant for multipolarity? / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• G20 is a forum of major economies —both developed and emerging —that coordinates
  • global economic policy-reflects multipolarity by including diverse powers like China, India,
  • and Brazil- reducing dominance of Western-led institutions like the G7.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: What are the three levels of analysis for the causes of war? / [CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Kenneth Waltz identified three levels of analysis for the causes of war- individual (human
  • nature, leaders), state (regime type, nationalism), and systemic (anarchic international
  • structure)-each level explains different dynamics influencing conflict and cooperation.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Analyze the five sectors of security identified by the Copenhagen School of Security Studies / [CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Copenhagen School defines five security sectors —military, political, economic, societal,
  • and environmental-these sectors highlight how threats can extend beyond armed conflict to
  • identity, stability, resources, and ecological sustainability, broadening the concept of security.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Explain the North–South divide in sustainable development debates. / [CO5] [5x6 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• North–South divide in sustainable development debates reflects inequalities where the
  • Global North emphasizes environmental protection, while the South prioritizes economic
  • growth and equity- underscores tensions between development needs and global ecological
  • responsibility.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: How does the UN Charter balance state sovereignty with the need for collective security? / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• UN Charter upholds state sovereignty through principles of equality and non-interference
  • while balancing it with collective security- Chapters VI and VII-allows the Security Council to
  • take collective action against threats to peace, emphasizing cooperation without permanently
  • undermining national independence or self-determination.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Discuss how Neo-Liberalism redefines the role of states in international politics through the lens of institutionalism. Use examples of international organizations to support your argument. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Neo -Liberalism redefines states as cooperative actors operating within institutional
  • frameworks-through institutionalism, it stresses that international organizations like the
  • WTO, IMF, and UN reduce anarchy by creating rules, transparency, and interdependence -
  • States pursue mutual gains through economic and political cooperation rather than solely
  • maximizing power or self-interest.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Examine polycentricity's conceptual evolution in IR. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Polycentricity in IR evolved from a state -centric to a multi -actor concept - recognizing
  • multiple centres of authority—states, organizations, corporations, and networks - highlights
  • the diffusion of power in global governance, where decision -making is shared across levels,
  • reflecting the rise of complex interdependence and multipolar world dynamics.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Explain the key principles of the Brundtland definition of sustainable development. / [CO5] [15x2 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• Brundtland definition of sustainable development emphasizes meeting present needs
  • without compromising future generations’ ability to meet theirs-integrates three principles—
  • economic growth, social equity, and environmental protection—promoting intergenerational
  • justice, resource conservation, and sustainable global partnerships for balanced human and
  • ecological well-being.
